name: ConvLSTM, LSTM and MLP neural network sequence models

identity.method_name: ConvLSTM (raster sequence), LSTM (scalar water-area sequence), and MLP (feed-forward, non-recurrent) neural networks applied to the project's 7-date-per-lake time series
identity.core_idea: ConvLSTM replaces the matrix multiplications inside an LSTM cell with convolutions, so it can take a stack of 2-D water-mask rasters (one per acquisition date) and learn spatio-temporal patterns, in principle predicting the next date's raster or classifying a pixel's trajectory. A plain LSTM does the same thing but on a single scalar per date (e.g. per-lake water area in hectares), treating each lake as one length-7 sequence. An MLP is not recurrent at all -- it maps a fixed-length input vector (e.g. 7 stacked area values, or a pixel's per-date reflectance vector) to an output in one shot, with no internal memory of order; it is included here because it is the architecture actually used in the closest domestic precedent (Karela oxbow lake study).
identity.official_dataset_ids: None. These are architectures, not datasets. They would consume the project's own derived series: per-lake MNDWI/NDVI water-area scalars (6 lakes x 7 years) or the 7-date water-mask raster stack per lake, both built from COPERNICUS Sentinel-2 L2A via Earth Search STAC (tile 43PGQ), which the project already holds.

fit_to_project.ground_truth_proxy_strategy: For pure next-step forecasting of water area or of the raster itself, the strategy is self-supervised: the label is simply the next time step's already-observed value, so no manual encroachment label is required to fit the recurrence. But the moment the output is asked to mean something -- 'this trend is encroachment' -- the same proxy problem the whole project has returns: there is no ground-truth encroachment label to validate the forecast against, so any downstream claim still rests on the same MNDWI/NDVI threshold rule already in use. Cost: zero extra labelling for the forecasting step itself, but zero added evidentiary weight for the encroachment claim either.
fit_to_project.input_required: LSTM/MLP-on-scalars: the 6x7 water-area matrix the project already computes from its MNDWI pipeline -- no acquisition needed. ConvLSTM: the full 7-date stack of per-lake water masks (or raw band stacks) at 20 m -- also already producible from the existing pipeline, just not yet organised as a rank-4 tensor (time, height, width, channel).
fit_to_project.viable_with_42_rows: No, for any architecture with recurrent/temporal structure. Reframing options and their real sample sizes: (a) per-lake scalar series -> 6 independent sequences of length 7 (not 42 -- the 42 'rows' are lake-years, not independent series; a sequence model needs whole sequences, and there are only 6). (b) per-pixel ConvLSTM -> ~900,000 pixels per scene look like a large N, but every pixel in a lake shares the same 7 time stamps and is spatially autocorrelated with its neighbours (they mostly flip water/not-water together at the shoreline), so the effective number of independent temporal trajectories is close to the number of lakes (6), not 900,000. Either way the usable count of genuinely independent 7-step sequences is 6. An LSTM/ConvLSTM with even a modest hidden size (32-64 units) has thousands to tens of thousands of trainable weights; fitting that to 6 sequences is textbook overfitting, not learning.
fit_to_project.viable_without_ground_truth: yes for the forecasting task itself (self-supervised, as above), but the forecast cannot be validated as an encroachment signal without ground truth, and n=6 sequences makes any validation split (e.g. leave-one-lake-out) statistically underpowered regardless.
fit_to_project.resolution_match_20m: Not a resolution problem -- ConvLSTM/LSTM/MLP are architecture-agnostic to input resolution and can run directly on the project's 20 m grid with no pretrained-weight mismatch (they would be trained from scratch on this data, not fine-tuned from a foundation model). The binding constraint here is temporal, not spatial: 7 time steps, not 20 m pixels.
fit_to_project.label_source_needed: None for next-step forecasting (self-supervised). If repurposed as a classifier of 'encroaching vs stable' lake, the label would have to come from the same MNDWI/NDVI threshold rule already used as the null baseline -- i.e., no new label source exists.
fit_to_project.fixes_which_stated_limitation: None of the four. It does not increase the 42-row count (limitation 1) -- it only reorganises the same 42 lake-years into 6 sequences, which is a worse effective sample size, not a better one. It does nothing about the OpenStreetMap building snapshot (limitation 2), does nothing about the missing ground truth (limitation 3), and does nothing about the one-scene-per-year dry-season-only sampling (limitation 4) -- a recurrent model over 7 dry-season points cannot recover the intra-annual variation that was never captured.
fit_to_project.handles_desilting_confound: No. With only 7 points per lake, a data-driven sequence model has no way to distinguish a genuine encroachment trend from Bellandur's engineered desilting cycle (15.7 ha in 2019 -> 0.4 ha in 2021 -> 107.9 ha in 2025) unless an exogenous 'desilting event' flag is manually added as an extra input feature -- at which point the model is not learning the confound away, a human is hand-coding it away, and 7 points is still too few to fit even a small extra parameter for that flag reliably.
fit_to_project.handles_hyacinth_confound: No. The sequence model only sees whatever the upstream MNDWI/NDVI masks already decided is 'water' vs 'vegetation'; it has no mechanism to re-examine misclassified hyacinth mats (Bellandur 2019: 16 ha water vs 260 ha vegetation inside a 315 ha footprint per Bhagyashree & Kumar/MDPI 2020, doi 10.3390/rs12223843). Feeding a bad water/vegetation split into a recurrent model just forecasts the bad split forward.
fit_to_project.legal_traceability: None. Output is a numeric forecast or a raster prediction with no cadastral or statutory meaning; it would still be measured only against the OpenStreetMap proxy polygon, never against the Bengaluru Master Plan 30 m buffer, the earlier NGT 75 m buffer, KTCDA records, or the National Wetland Atlas. No buffer distance is being tested by this method at all.
fit_to_project.temporal_granularity: This is the field the method lives or dies on. Every one of the project's 6 lakes contributes exactly 7 values, one per year, each representing a single dry-season snapshot (limitation 4). LSTM and ConvLSTM are designed for tasks with tens to hundreds of time steps so the network can learn what 'normal' temporal dynamics look like before generalising; with 7 points there is no slack left to separate signal from single-lake idiosyncrasy. The MLP-Markov style precedent (see evidence) does not actually rely on many time steps either -- it substitutes many per-pixel training samples drawn from just 2 land-cover maps at a time for the small number of true calendar dates, which is a fundamentally different way of buying sample size that this project's raster stack could in principle borrow (see recommended_rank), but doing so abandons the 'sequence model' framing entirely.

implementation.libraries: Python: TensorFlow/Keras (tf.keras.layers.ConvLSTM2D, LSTM, Dense) or PyTorch (torch.nn.LSTM, custom ConvLSTM cell -- no first-party ConvLSTM in core PyTorch); scikit-learn MLPRegressor as a lighter-weight MLP option. No specialised remote-sensing library is required since this is generic sequence modelling once the raster/scalar tensors are built.
implementation.pretrained_weights: None exist for this task. There is no public ConvLSTM/LSTM checkpoint pretrained on lake water-area or water-mask sequences at any resolution; every use here would mean training from scratch on the project's own 6-42 data points, which is precisely the problem, not a workaround for it.
implementation.licence: Apache 2.0 / BSD (TensorFlow, PyTorch, scikit-learn) -- no restriction for academic use.
implementation.compute_requirement: Trivial to run on a laptop CPU -- the datasets are tiny (a handful of KB of scalars, or at most a few hundred MB of rasters), and training 'completes' (i.e. overfits) in seconds to a couple of minutes. No GPU or Colab/Kaggle quota is actually needed; the constraint is statistical, not computational.
implementation.student_days: 1-2 days to implement the LSTM/MLP-on-scalars version and honestly document that it fails to generalise under leave-one-lake-out; add 2-3 more days if attempting the ConvLSTM raster version (tensor plumbing, memory handling for 6x7x~900x~1000 stacks, and again documenting the same negative result). Total 3-5 student-days for a method whose expected deliverable is a documented null result, not a working forecaster.

evaluation.metrics: MAE / RMSE of the predicted next-year water area against the observed value would be the nominal metric, but with only 6 independent sequences these numbers have no statistical power -- a single unlucky held-out lake (e.g. Bellandur, mid-desilting) can swing the reported error by an order of magnitude. Accuracy alone is meaningless here; the metric that actually matters is whether the model generalises at all across lakes, which the data cannot show either way with n=6.
evaluation.validation_protocol: leave-one-lake-out is the only defensible split (train on 5 lakes' 7-point series, test on the 6th), never a naive shuffled k-fold, which would let a model memorise a lake's other years and leak lake identity. Note that leave-one-lake-out here means only 6 folds of 1 test sequence each -- the smallest possible cross-validation, essentially a demonstration rather than a statistically meaningful estimate of generalisation error.
evaluation.leakage_risk: Two independent leakage channels. (1) Lake-identity leakage: if any pooled/shuffled split is used instead of leave-one-lake-out, the model sees other years of the same lake in training and trivially 'predicts' the held-out year from lake-specific level, not from a learned temporal pattern. (2) Spatial autocorrelation in the ConvLSTM/per-pixel reframing: neighbouring pixels within the same lake-year are not independent samples, so treating them as if they multiply the effective sample size (as in viable_with_42_rows) is itself a leakage-adjacent statistical error that would inflate any pixel-level accuracy number.
evaluation.uncertainty_reporting: None inherent to a point-forecast LSTM/ConvLSTM/MLP. A bootstrap or conformal interval built from only 6 sequences would itself be built on too few resamples to be trustworthy (bootstrapping n=6 typically just reproduces close variants of the same 6 curves). With no ground truth and 6 sequences, any confidence interval quoted here should be treated as illustrative at best, and the panel should be told that explicitly rather than shown a number without that caveat.
evaluation.augmentation_honesty_risk: High if attempted. Because 6 sequences of length 7 are obviously too few, the natural next move is to synthetically lengthen or multiply them (interpolating extra 'years', GAN- or diffusion-based time-series augmentation, or jittering pixel rasters to manufacture more ConvLSTM training examples). Any of these can fabricate a plausible-looking encroachment trend that is actually an artefact of the augmentation prior, not of the Sentinel-2 record. If augmentation is used at all, it must be disclosed in the same figure/table as the result, with the real (n=6) and augmented (n=synthetic) counts both stated, and the result should not be reported as if it came from real observations.

evidence.published_performance: Karela oxbow lake study (Dutta, Kushwaha & Dubey, 2026, Environmental Monitoring and Assessment, doi 10.1007/s10661-026-15043-4): reports a 90.64% decrease in wetland area for Karela Lake, Lucknow, over 1976-2024 (48 years), using an MLP neural network. [verify] The abstract and available metadata (PubMed ID 41619067, Semantic Scholar record) confirm the MLP-NN role and the headline shrinkage figure, but the full text is paywalled, so the exact number of training samples fed to the MLP could not be directly confirmed. Based on how MLP is used in essentially every comparable Indian LULC-change study of this type (MLP as the transition-potential sub-model inside a CA-Markov / Land Change Modeler workflow, e.g. IDRISI TerrSet), the MLP is almost certainly trained on per-pixel land-cover transition samples drawn from a handful of classified LULC maps (likely 4-6 dates across 1976-2024), not on '48 yearly observations' as a sequence. That per-pixel training set would run to thousands or tens of thousands of samples -- vastly larger than this project's 42 lake-years, and structurally a different sampling unit entirely (pixel-transition classification, not time-series forecasting). [uncertain] This is the central finding to report honestly: the paper is not actually a small-sample precedent for a sequence model at comparable n; it is a large-per-pixel-sample precedent for a completely different (cross-sectional, not recurrent) use of an MLP, and its headline 90.64% figure is a LULC classification/change-detection result, not a validated multi-year forecast.
evidence.study_area_of_that_work: Single lake (Karela, an oxbow of the Gomti/Ganga basin, southern Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh), a peri-urban/rural wetland, not an urban lake series; one lake studied over 48 years with a handful of classified LULC map dates, contrasted with this project's 6 urban lakes x 7 near-annual dates. Not comparable in scale, in urban context, or in what the neural network was actually asked to do.
evidence.applies_to_indian_urban_lakes: Partially. The Karela study is Indian and wetland-focused but is not Bengaluru and is not a sequence model over annual water-area values -- it is an MLP-based land-cover transition model. No published ConvLSTM or LSTM application specifically to Bengaluru lake water-area or water-mask time series was found. General (non-deep-learning) Bengaluru lake LULC change studies exist, e.g. the Yele Mallappa Shetty lake series study (Environmental Monitoring and Assessment, doi 10.1007/s10661-024-13153-5) and Ramachandra-group remote-sensing LULC work, but these use classical classification/change-detection, not recurrent neural networks. [verify]
evidence.evidence_recency: 2026 (Karela study, the strongest and most on-topic precedent found). General ConvLSTM-for-satellite-time-series literature (e.g. MODIS vegetation-health-index ConvLSTM forecasting, PMC10923737, 2024) is 2020-2024 and uses dense multi-decade dekadal/monthly series (hundreds of time steps), which is the opposite data regime from this project's 7 points and should not be read as supporting evidence for feasibility here.
evidence.primary_sources: Karela oxbow lake study: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10661-026-15043-4 (doi:10.1007/s10661-026-15043-4); PubMed record https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41619067/. Bellandur/Varthur macrophyte mapping cross-check: MDPI Remote Sensing 2020, doi:10.3390/rs12223843. ConvLSTM-for-remote-sensing-time-series context: 'Next-level vegetation health index forecasting: A ConvLSTM study using MODIS Time Series', PMC10923737, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10923737/. General note on ConvLSTM scaling limits with long/large sequences: Bytez summary of arXiv:2506.14362, https://bytez.com/docs/arxiv/2506.14362/paper. Bengaluru lake series LULC precedent (classical, not DL): doi:10.1007/s10661-024-13153-5.

risk.failure_modes: With 6 sequences and a network of even modest capacity, the model will simply memorise each training lake's 7-point curve rather than learn a generalisable temporal pattern; leave-one-lake-out testing will then produce wildly lake-dependent errors (a held-out Bellandur, mid-desilting-cycle, will look like total model failure; a held-out stable lake will look artificially good). Any 'trend' the model reports for a confound-heavy lake (desilting, hyacinth) will be presented with the same confidence as a trend for a clean lake, because the architecture has no mechanism to know the difference.
risk.panel_defensibility: The first question a panel will ask is 'how many independent sequences did you train this on?' The honest answer, 6, immediately undercuts any claim that the recurrent model learned something rather than memorised something. There is no defensible answer to 'how do you know that forecast is real when you have no ground truth and six data points?' -- the method does not survive that question, and presenting it as a primary result invites the panel to reject the whole modelling section on credibility grounds rather than just this one method.
risk.honest_expectation: This will not produce a validated, generalising sequence model. At best it can be shown as an explicitly-labelled toy/negative-result exercise (e.g., 'we attempted an LSTM over the 7-year series and it overfits by construction, which we demonstrate and use to justify a classical trend method instead'). A null result here -- 'sequence models are not trainable on this data' -- is the scientifically honest and reportable conclusion; a classical alternative (linear regression, Sen's slope / Mann-Kendall trend test, or simple year-over-year percentage change) needs far fewer assumptions, is transparent about its own limits, and should be the actual deliverable in this space instead.

verdict.recommended_rank: reject -- as a primary deep-learning model, ConvLSTM/LSTM cannot be trained meaningfully on 6 sequences of length 7 without overfitting or fabricating a trend via synthetic augmentation; consider-with-reasons only as a deliberately-labelled negative-result exercise, or as a repurposed non-sequence MLP pixel classifier trained within a single scene (thousands of pixel samples, following the Karela precedent's actual mechanism) -- but that use case is really a deep-learning-image classifier, not a sequence model, and duplicates work the project's existing MNDWI/NDVI rule already does more transparently.
verdict.one_line_for_the_guide: There are only 6 independent 7-step lake time series in this dataset -- not enough to train any recurrent model without it memorising or overfitting -- so instead of ConvLSTM/LSTM I used a classical trend method and report the small-sample limitation explicitly, citing the Karela MLP study as a precedent that actually relied on large per-pixel samples, not a comparably small n.
